sections.DIVE: Project deep dive and behavioural prompts

cards.title: Bias vs variance
cards.question: Define bias and variance. Which way does a linear model lean versus a deep net?
cards.answer:
• Bias: error from a model too simple to capture the true pattern; systematic, like a straight line through curved data.
• Variance: error from sensitivity to the particular training sample; retrain on a new sample and the model changes a lot. High-capacity models can memorize training-set quirks.
• Linear regression: high bias, low variance. Deep nets: low bias, high variance by default, controlled with regularization, dropout, more data.
• For an estimator, MSE = bias^2 + variance. Prediction error also has an irreducible floor (the Bayes error) that no model removes.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Overparameterized nets often generalize despite huge capacity. Mention double descent and implicit regularization from SGD noise (small-batch gradient noise pushes training toward flatter minima, which generalize better), and that the classic U-curve is not the whole story.
cards.note: Variance is model sensitivity, not a property of the data

cards.title: L1 vs L2
cards.question: Write both penalized losses. Why does L1 give exact zeros and L2 does not?
cards.answer:
• L2: base_loss + lambda * sum(w_j^2). L1: base_loss + lambda * sum(|w_j|). Both are added.
• Penalty gradient: L2 = 2 * lambda * w_j (shrinks as w shrinks, never reaches 0). L1 = lambda * sign(w_j) (constant push until exactly 0).
• Full gradient per weight = base loss gradient + penalty gradient; each weight is penalized independently.
• Closed form (quadratic loss, diagonal Hessian H): L1 gives w_i = sign(w*_i) * max(|w*_i| - lambda / H_ii, 0), so any weight whose unpenalized optimum is small lands exactly at 0. L2 gives w_i = H_ii / (H_ii + 2 * lambda) * w*_i, never 0 if w*_i is not.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Correlated features: L1 (Lasso) tends to pick one of them at random; L2 (ridge) shrinks them together and is more robust to collinearity. Elastic net combines both and tends to keep both.

cards.title: Train vs validation gap
cards.question: Training error low, validation error high. Diagnosis?
cards.answer:
• Overfitting: the gap between training and test error is too large; the model has learned training-set specifics that do not generalize.
• Fixes: more data, regularization, smaller model, early stopping, augmentation.
cards.key_concept: Probe — The overfitting diagnosis assumes train and validation are drawn i.i.d. from the same distribution. If validation data comes from a different distribution, the gap can be dataset mismatch, not overfitting. Hold out a slice of the training distribution: if the model does well on that slice and badly on validation, the problem is the shift.

cards.title: Underfitting
cards.question: Both training and validation error high. Diagnosis and fixes?
cards.answer:
• Underfitting: the model cannot get training error low enough. Causes: too little capacity, optimization failure (e.g., a badly tuned learning rate), weak features, too much regularization.
• Fixes: bigger or different model, tune the learning rate and optimizer, better features, lower regularization.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How do you tell it apart from noisy labels? Compare against the Bayes error, estimated for example by human-level performance. If large, well-tuned models still plateau, the problem may be data that is too noisy or inputs that lack the needed information, not capacity.

cards.title: Generative vs discriminative
cards.question: Formal distinction, and how it differs from the buzzword "generative AI."
cards.answer:
• Generative: models the joint P(x, y) or P(x). Examples: Naive Bayes, LLMs (autoregressive: an explicit P(x) via the chain rule), GANs (they sample from P(x) without an explicit density).
• Discriminative: models only P(y | x), or a direct map from x to the label. Example: logistic regression.
• "Generative AI" colloquially means the task generates content. Naive Bayes is formally generative but is a classifier.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Ng and Jordan: generative models can converge faster with little data, discriminative models usually win asymptotically.
cards.note: Formal definition is about what is modeled

cards.title: Parametric vs non-parametric
cards.question: Define each. Why does adding features to linear regression not make it non-parametric?
cards.answer:
• Parametric: fixed form, parameter vector whose size is fixed before any data is observed (linear regression, logistic regression).
• Non-parametric: effective complexity grows with the number of observations (KNN, decision trees allowed to grow to arbitrary size).
• Adding features is a design change before training. The question is growth with observations.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Trees are non-parametric in form but are usually regularized with size constraints (max depth, min leaf size) that make them parametric in practice.

cards.title: Bagging vs boosting
cards.question: Mechanism and bias/variance effect of each.
cards.answer:
• Bagging (random forest): independent models in parallel on bootstrap samples (drawn with replacement), averaged or voted. Reduces variance because uncorrelated errors average out; unlike boosting it is not designed to reduce bias. Random forests also pick a random subset of features at each split to decorrelate trees.
• Boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM): sequential models, each added to correct the current ensemble's errors. Can reduce bias (builds a higher-capacity ensemble); can overfit without shrinkage and regularization.
• Mnemonic: Bagging = Both vote together, balances variance. Boosting = Building on mistakes, chips at bias.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why does decorrelation matter? With n models of error variance sigma^2 and pairwise correlation rho, the ensemble's expected squared error is rho * sigma^2 + (1 - rho) * sigma^2 / n, so correlation rho sets a floor that more trees cannot remove.
cards.note: Core right (bagging cuts variance, boosting cuts bias; bootstrap with replacement needed a nudge). Missed the probe: Var = rho*sigma^2 + (1-rho)*sigma^2/n, correlation sets a floor, so feature subsampling decorrelates trees. Recited it back cleanly after teaching but not solid cold. Say pairwise correlation.

cards.title: Curse of dimensionality
cards.question: What is it, why does it happen, and why does it hurt KNN?
cards.answer:
• A side effect of many features. The number of cells to cover grows exponentially: covering 10% per axis covers 10% in 1D, 1% in 2D, 10^-100 in 100D. A fixed dataset becomes extremely sparse: most cells have no training example.
• Distances concentrate: nearest and farthest neighbors end up at similar distances, so "nearest" loses meaning.
• KNN depends entirely on distance. Mitigate by keeping only meaningful dimensions (PCA, feature selection) or with learned embeddings.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why do embeddings in 128 to 768 dimensions still work for retrieval? Real data lies near a low-dimensional manifold, so its intrinsic dimensionality is far below the nominal one (where Beyer et al. say nearest neighbor stays meaningful), and embeddings are trained (e.g., contrastively) so that similarity is meaningful along it.
cards.note: Started with volume and compute; corrected to sparsity then distance concentration (nearest and farthest become about equally far, so nearest neighbor loses meaning). Probe: embeddings work because data lies on a low-dimensional manifold and training makes distance meaningful. Open: PCA is linear, autoencoder is the nonlinear version.

cards.title: MLE vs MAP
cards.question: Define both. How do they connect to regularization?
cards.answer:
• MLE: choose parameters maximizing P(data | theta). In practice minimize negative log-likelihood.
• MAP: maximize P(theta | data), proportional to P(data | theta) * P(theta). Adds a log-prior term.
• Gaussian prior on weights gives L2; Laplace prior gives L1.
• MSE is the MLE under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the MLE under a Bernoulli or categorical model.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why log-likelihood? Products of probabilities underflow; logs turn them into sums and keep the same argmax.

cards.title: Logistic regression
cards.question: Loss, gradient, and why not MSE?
cards.answer:
• p = sigmoid(w^T x). Loss = -[y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p)].
• Gradient = (p - y) * x. Clean, and the loss is convex.
• MSE with a sigmoid saturates: its gradient includes p(1 - p), which vanishes when the model is confidently wrong.
• Coefficients are log-odds changes per unit of the feature.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Perfectly separable data: weights blow up to infinity without regularization.

cards.title: Softmax, cross-entropy, KL
cards.question: How are cross-entropy and KL divergence related? What does label smoothing do?
cards.answer:
• Cross-entropy H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q). With fixed true labels, minimizing cross-entropy equals minimizing KL.
• Softmax plus cross-entropy gradient w.r.t. logits = q - p.
• Label smoothing mixes the one-hot target with a uniform distribution: each of the K classes gets epsilon / K and the true class gets 1 - epsilon + epsilon / K. Reduces overconfidence, often helps calibration and generalization.
• KL is asymmetric: forward KL(p || q) is mass-covering, reverse KL(q || p) is mode-seeking.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Where does reverse KL show up? Variational inference (maximizing the ELBO minimizes KL(q || p)), and the KL penalty to the reference policy in RLHF, KL(pi_theta || pi_ref).

cards.title: Gradient boosting mechanics
cards.question: How does gradient boosting actually fit each tree? What do XGBoost and LightGBM add?
cards.answer:
• Each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss w.r.t. current predictions (pseudo-residuals). For MSE that is the plain residual.
• Shrinkage (learning rate) scales each tree's contribution.
• XGBoost: second-order Taylor expansion (gradient and Hessian), L2 on leaf weights, a per-leaf penalty gamma, a closed-form split gain, sparsity-aware splits.
• LightGBM: histogram binning, leaf-wise (best-first) growth (lower loss for a fixed leaf count, can overfit small data, cap with max_depth), GOSS sampling, exclusive feature bundling.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why do GBDTs still beat deep nets on medium-sized (~10K-sample) tabular data? Heterogeneous features, irregular target functions that NNs struggle to learn, robustness to uninformative features, and NNs' rotation invariance (trees respect the data's orientation). Deep nets win when you have huge sparse ID features and need learned embeddings.

cards.title: Trees and feature importance
cards.question: How do trees choose splits? Why is impurity-based feature importance misleading?
cards.answer:
• Classification: maximize reduction in Gini or entropy. Regression: maximize variance (MSE) reduction.
• Impurity importance (MDI) is computed on training data, so it can credit features that do not predict on unseen data when the model overfits, and it is biased toward high-cardinality (typically numerical) features.
• Prefer permutation importance on a holdout, or SHAP.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Permutation importance also misleads with correlated features, since permuting one leaves its twin intact and both look less important. Cluster correlated features and keep one per cluster.

cards.title: Cross-validation
cards.question: When is k-fold CV wrong, and what do you use instead?
cards.answer:
• Time series: random folds leak the future. Use forward-chaining splits (e.g., TimeSeriesSplit: each training set is a superset of the previous one and the test fold comes after it).
• Grouped data (users, sessions): put all rows of a group in the same fold, or you measure memorization of group-specific features.
• Hyperparameter tuning plus evaluation on the same folds is optimistic; use nested CV or a final untouched test set.
cards.key_concept: Probe — In production you typically evaluate on data gathered after the training window, because that better reflects what the system will do live, then confirm with an online A/B test.

cards.title: Data leakage
cards.question: Name the main kinds of leakage and how you catch them.
cards.answer:
• Target leakage: a feature computed from or after the label (for example "refund issued" predicting fraud).
• Temporal leakage: training on data from after the prediction time, or aggregates that include the future.
• Preprocessing leakage: fitting scalers, imputers, or target encoders on the full dataset before splitting.
• Entity leakage: the same user (or other group) in both train and test.
• Detection: suspiciously high offline metrics, a big offline-online gap.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Point-in-time correct feature joins (DATA-02) are the systematic fix: they reproduce each feature's value as of the label's timestamp.

cards.title: Class imbalance techniques
cards.question: How do you handle a 0.1% positive rate?
cards.answer:
• Data level: downsample negatives (can speed up training and improve the model) or oversample positives.
• Loss level: class weights (e.g., inverse class frequency), focal loss (down-weights easy examples by (1 - p_t)^gamma, where p_t is the probability of the true class).
• Evaluation: PR curve and PR-AUC (more informative than ROC under imbalance), recall at fixed precision, cost-based thresholds.
• If you downsample, correct the predicted probabilities afterward (ADS-03).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Weighting and resampling shift the effective base rate, so they change calibration. If downstream uses the probability (auctions, expected cost), recalibrate.

cards.title: Calibration
cards.question: What is calibration, how do you measure it, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer:
• Calibrated: among predictions of 0.3, about 30% are positive.
• Measure: reliability diagram, expected calibration error, calibration ratio (sum of predictions / sum of labels), log loss (mixes calibration with discrimination).
• Fix: Platt scaling (logistic fit on scores), isotonic regression (non-parametric, needs more data, roughly 1000+ samples), temperature scaling for neural nets.
• Matters when the probability is consumed directly: ad auctions (bids weighted by pCTR-based quality scores), expected-cost thresholds.
cards.key_concept: Probe — AUC measures ranking without considering calibration (a global 0.5x multiplier leaves it unchanged). A model can have great AUC and terrible calibration, which breaks an auction.

cards.title: PCA
cards.question: What does PCA compute and what are its limits?
cards.answer:
• Finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance: eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (X^T X for centered X), computed in practice via SVD of centered data.
• Keep the top k components by explained variance.
• Limits: linear only, sensitive to scaling (it centers but does not scale features, so standardize first), unsupervised so variance is not the same as predictive usefulness.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Autoencoders give non-linear dimensionality reduction; a linear autoencoder with MSE recovers the PCA subspace.

cards.title: K-means
cards.question: Objective, algorithm, and failure modes.
cards.answer:
• Minimizes within-cluster sum of squared distances (inertia). Lloyd's algorithm alternates assignment and centroid updates; always converges, but possibly to a local optimum.
• k-means++ initialization spreads initial centroids and improves results.
• Assumes convex, isotropic clusters of similar variance: fails on elongated or irregular shapes and on clusters with very different spreads. Choosing k: silhouette analysis, downstream task.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Where does k-means show up in production ML? IVF indexes for ANN search (REC-04) and product quantization codebooks.

cards.title: Bayes and base rates
cards.question: A fraud model has 99% recall and a 1% false positive rate. Fraud prevalence is 0.1%. If it flags a transaction, how likely is it fraud?
cards.answer:
• P(fraud | flag) = (0.99 * 0.001) / (0.99 * 0.001 + 0.01 * 0.999) ≈ 0.00099 / 0.01098 ≈ 9%.
• Low prevalence makes even a good false positive rate produce mostly false alarms. This is precision.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What do you change? Raise the threshold, add a second-stage model, or route flags to human review sized for that volume.

cards.title: CLT and standard error
cards.question: What does the CLT say and why does it matter for experiments?
cards.answer:
• The sampling distribution of a mean of many independent samples approaches normal, whatever the underlying distribution (finite variance).
• Standard error of the mean = sigma / sqrt(n). Halving the error needs 4x the data.
• Justifies normal-approximation (z) tests and confidence intervals on metrics like average watch time.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Heavy-tailed, skewed metrics (revenue) need many more users before the mean is close to normal (Kohavi's rule of thumb: 355 x skewness^2 per variant). Cap or transform the metric to reduce skewness before testing.

cards.title: Hypothesis testing
cards.question: Define a p-value precisely, and type I and type II errors.
cards.answer:
• p-value: the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. Not the probability the null is true.
• Type I: false positive, rate alpha. Type II: false negative, rate beta. Power = 1 - beta.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Statistically significant is not practically significant. Report effect size and a confidence interval.

cards.title: Bootstrap
cards.question: What is the bootstrap and when do you use it?
cards.answer:
• Resample the data with replacement many times, compute the statistic each time, and use that distribution for confidence intervals.
• Use when the statistic has no simple variance formula: medians, percentiles, ratio metrics. It gets expensive on big data, where the delta method gives closed-form alternatives.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Resample the randomization unit (users), not rows, or you understate variance.

cards.title: Multiple comparisons
cards.question: You test 20 metrics at alpha 0.05. What goes wrong and how do you fix it?
cards.answer:
• Expect about one false positive by chance.
• Bonferroni: alpha / m, controls family-wise error, conservative.
• Benjamini-Hochberg: controls the false discovery rate, more power.
• Practical: pre-register one primary metric; treat the rest as guardrails or exploratory.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Many simultaneous experiments and segments ("it won for Android users in Brazil") are the same problem in disguise.

cards.title: Gradient descent variants
cards.question: Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch. Tradeoffs?
cards.answer:
• Batch: exact gradient over all data; slow per step, memory heavy.
• SGD: one example; noisy, cheap, noise can help escape sharp minima.
• Mini-batch: the default; vectorizes on GPUs, balances noise and stability.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Very large batches can hurt generalization (they tend to converge to sharp minima) and need learning-rate scaling (linear scaling rule with warmup) or layerwise adaptive optimizers (LARS/LAMB).

cards.title: Momentum, Adam, AdamW
cards.question: How do momentum and Adam work? Why is AdamW not the same as Adam with L2?
cards.answer:
• Momentum: exponential average of gradients; smooths updates, speeds through ravines.
• Adam: first moment m (momentum) and second moment v (squared gradients), with bias correction; update = lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps). Per-parameter adaptive steps.
• With L2 inside Adam, the decay gradient is divided by sqrt(v), so parameters with large gradients get less decay. AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights, decoupled from the adaptive scaling.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Adam's memory cost: two extra fp32 states per parameter, which matters for LLM training (DIST-04).

cards.title: Learning-rate schedules and warmup
cards.question: Why warm up? Why cosine decay?
cards.answer:
• Warmup: early on the network changes rapidly and Adam's adaptive learning rate has high variance (too few samples seen), so big steps destabilize training. The original Transformer and large-batch SGD both use it.
• Decay (cosine, linear, step): SGD's gradient noise does not vanish even at a minimum, so the learning rate must shrink over time to settle.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Loss spikes mid-training in LLMs: PaLM saw them despite gradient clipping and mitigated them by restarting from a checkpoint about 100 steps before the spike and skipping roughly 200-500 batches.

cards.title: Initialization
cards.question: Why does initialization matter? Xavier vs He.
cards.answer:
• Bad scale makes activations and gradients explode or vanish across layers.
• Xavier/Glorot: variance 2 / (fan_in + fan_out), a compromise between preserving forward and backward variance; derived for roughly linear units, tested with tanh.
• He: variance 2 / fan_in; compensates ReLU zeroing half its inputs.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why not initialize all weights to zero? Symmetry: every neuron in a layer gets the same gradient and stays identical.

cards.title: Dropout
cards.question: How does dropout behave at train vs inference time?
cards.answer:
• Training: zero each activation with probability p. Inverted dropout scales survivors by 1 / (1 - p) so expected values match.
• Inference: no dropout, no scaling needed.
• Interpretation: trains an implicit ensemble of subnetworks; discourages co-adaptation.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Large LLM pretraining often uses no dropout (PaLM; nanoGPT defaults to 0.0): it is about one pass over a huge corpus, with repetition avoided to limit overfitting. Dropout around 0.1 comes back for fine-tuning.

cards.title: Exploding gradients
cards.question: Causes and fixes.
cards.answer:
• Products of large derivatives across layers or time steps, too-high learning rates, bad initialization.
• Fixes: gradient clipping by global norm, lower LR, normalization layers, careful (normalized) init.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Clipping by global norm rescales all gradients jointly, so each step keeps the gradient direction. Clipping by value per element changes the direction, though experiments suggest both work similarly.

cards.title: Mixed precision
cards.question: fp16 vs bf16, and why loss scaling?
cards.answer:
• fp16: 5 exponent bits, small range; small gradients underflow to zero, so you multiply the loss by a scale factor and unscale before the update.
• bf16: 8 exponent bits, same range as fp32, less precision; usually no loss scaling needed. Default for matrix multiplies on TPUs.
• Keep fp32 master weights and optimizer states for stable updates.
cards.key_concept: Probe — fp8 training is emerging; some networks need per-tensor scaling factors, and the outputs of fp8 matrix multiplies are kept in higher precision.

cards.title: Regularization toolbox
cards.question: List regularization methods beyond L1 and L2.
cards.answer: • Dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, weight decay, label smoothing, mixup and cutmix, smaller models, ensembling, noise injection, stochastic depth.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Early stopping is roughly equivalent to L2 regularization for linear models with gradient descent.

cards.title: Vanishing gradient
cards.question: What is it, why does it happen, and what fixes it?
cards.answer:
• Backprop multiplies derivatives through layers; if they are mostly under 1 (sigmoid, tanh saturate), the product shrinks exponentially and early layers barely learn.
• Fixes: ReLU-family activations, residual connections, normalization, good initialization, LSTM gating for sequences.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why do residual connections fix it? The identity path gives the gradient a route with derivative 1 straight to earlier layers.

cards.title: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm
cards.question: Which axis does each normalize over, and where is each used?
cards.answer:
• BatchNorm: per feature, across examples in the mini-batch. Depends on batch size; uses running statistics at inference. Common in CNNs.
• LayerNorm: per example, across features. Batch-independent. Standard in transformers.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Pre-LN vs post-LN transformers: pre-LN (normalize before attention and MLP) trains more stably and needs less warmup. RMSNorm drops mean-centering and is common in modern LLMs.

cards.title: Residual connections
cards.question: Why do residual connections let you train very deep networks?
cards.answer:
• Output = x + F(x). Layers learn a correction to the identity, which is easy to make near zero.
• Gradients flow through the identity path, avoiding vanishing.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Transformers rely on them as a "residual stream" that every layer reads from and writes to, which is also how interpretability research frames the model.

cards.title: Activations
cards.question: ReLU, dying ReLU, GELU, SwiGLU.
cards.answer:
• ReLU: max(0, x); no saturation for positives, so derivatives stay large while the unit is active. Dying ReLU: a unit gets no gradient on examples where it outputs 0, so it can get stuck if pushed negative; Leaky ReLU (a nonzero slope for negatives) helps.
• GELU: smooth, x * Phi(x); common in BERT and GPT.
• SwiGLU: gated linear unit with a Swish gate; used in many modern LLM MLP blocks (e.g. LLaMA), better quality at matched parameters and compute.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why are sigmoids still used? Output layers for probabilities and gates inside LSTMs and GLUs.

cards.title: CNNs
cards.question: What inductive biases do CNNs encode?
cards.answer:
• Locality (small kernels), weight sharing (same filter everywhere), translation equivariance; pooling adds some invariance.
• Receptive field grows with depth.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Vision transformers have weaker inductive bias, so they need more data or pretraining but scale better.

cards.title: RNNs and LSTMs
cards.question: How do LSTMs address vanishing gradients, and why did transformers replace them?
cards.answer:
• LSTM: a cell state with a linear self-loop, controlled by forget, input, and output gates, so information and gradients persist over many steps (the forget gate was a later addition, Gers et al. 2000).
• Transformers: parallel across the sequence during training, a constant number of operations between any two positions, and much less training time.
cards.key_concept: Probe — State-space models (Mamba) revisit recurrence for linear-time long sequences.

cards.title: Embeddings
cards.question: What is an embedding table, and how do you handle billions of IDs?
cards.answer:
• A learned lookup from a categorical ID to a dense vector, trained end to end.
• High cardinality: hashing trick (collisions trade accuracy for memory), dropping infrequent IDs, compositional embeddings (several smaller tables combined into a unique vector per ID, e.g. quotient-remainder).
• Embedding tables can dominate recsys model size; they are sharded across machines (DIST-06).
cards.key_concept: Probe — New IDs have untrained embeddings: fall back to content features (cold start, REC-06).

cards.title: Contrastive learning
cards.question: Explain InfoNCE and in-batch negatives.
cards.answer:
• Pull positive pairs together, push negatives apart. InfoNCE: softmax (cross-entropy) over similarity of the positive vs negatives, divided by temperature tau.
• In-batch negatives: other examples in the batch serve as negatives; bigger batches give more negatives (CLIP used 32,768).
• Lower temperature sharpens the distribution and focuses on hard negatives.
• Examples: CLIP (image-text), SimCLR, two-tower retrieval.
cards.key_concept: Probe — In-batch negatives oversample popular items; correct with logQ (DATA-03).

cards.title: Knowledge distillation
cards.question: How does distillation work and why use it?
cards.answer:
• Train a small student to match a large teacher's softened outputs (softmax at temperature T), often mixed with the true-label loss.
• Soft targets carry information about class similarity: the relative probabilities of wrong classes (a BMW is rarely mistaken for a garbage truck, but far more often than for a carrot).
• Use: meet serving latency and compute budgets the large model cannot.
cards.key_concept: Probe — The T^2 factor keeps gradient magnitudes comparable when using a temperature.

cards.title: Self-attention
cards.question: Write scaled dot-product attention. Why divide by sqrt(d_k)?
cards.answer:
• Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V, with Q, K, V linear projections of the input.
• Dot products of random d_k-dimensional vectors have variance about d_k. Without scaling, logits grow large, softmax saturates, and gradients vanish.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Decoder models add a causal mask (negative infinity above the diagonal) so position i cannot see later tokens.

cards.title: Multi-head, MQA, GQA
cards.question: Why multiple heads? What are multi-query and grouped-query attention for?
cards.answer:
• Multiple heads attend to different subspaces and relations in parallel.
• MQA: all query heads share one K and V head. GQA: query heads share K and V within groups.
• Purpose: shrink the KV cache and memory bandwidth at inference. MQA can lose quality; GQA is the middle ground, with quality close to multi-head and speed close to MQA.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Quantify it: GQA with 8 KV heads instead of 64 cuts KV cache memory 8x.

cards.title: Positional encoding
cards.question: Sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, ALiBi.
cards.answer:
• Self-attention without position information is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the input tokens and the outputs shuffle the same way, so word order carries no signal. Position must be injected.
• Sinusoidal: fixed functions added to embeddings. Learned: trainable vectors, with no way to encode positions beyond the training length.
• RoPE: rotates Q and K by position-dependent angles so their dot product depends on relative position. Used by the LLaMA, GPT-NeoX and PaLM families; context extension via scaling tricks.
• ALiBi: adds a linear distance penalty to attention logits; extrapolates well.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Long-context extension methods (position interpolation, YaRN) rescale RoPE positions or frequencies, then fine-tune briefly (PI: within 1000 steps).

cards.title: Attention cost and FlashAttention
cards.question: What is the complexity of attention, and what does FlashAttention change?
cards.answer:
• Time O(n^2 d), memory O(n^2) to materialize the attention matrix.
• FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles held in fast on-chip SRAM, with an online softmax, never writing the n x n matrix to HBM. Memory O(n), much faster because attention is memory-bandwidth bound.
• It is exact, not an approximation.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Approximate methods (sparse, linear attention) reduce FLOPs but trade off quality and often give no wall-clock speedup; IO-awareness was the missing practical win.

cards.title: Architectures
cards.question: Encoder-only vs decoder-only vs encoder-decoder.
cards.answer:
• Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional, masked-LM pretraining; strong for classification, question answering, and as the encoder for embeddings and retrieval.
• Decoder-only (GPT-style; InstructGPT is a fine-tuned GPT-3): causal, next-token prediction; generation, and loss scales predictably.
• Encoder-decoder (original Transformer, T5, BART): encoder reads input, decoder generates with cross-attention; translation and other seq2seq tasks.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why did decoder-only win for general LLMs? The next-token objective learns from every token (masked LM predicts only 15%), and its loss improves as a smooth power law with scale.

cards.title: Tokenization
cards.question: How does BPE work, and what problems does tokenization cause?
cards.answer:
• BPE: start from bytes or characters, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocab size is reached.
• Problems: arithmetic and spelling (numbers and words split oddly), non-English text costs more tokens per word (cost and context length), glitch tokens.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Vocab size tradeoff: bigger vocab means shorter sequences but a larger embedding and output softmax.

cards.title: Pretraining objective and perplexity
cards.question: What is the pretraining loss, and what is perplexity?
cards.answer:
• Next-token cross-entropy averaged over tokens.
• Perplexity = exp(average negative log-likelihood per token): the effective number of equally likely choices.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Perplexity is not comparable across different tokenizers, and lower perplexity does not guarantee better downstream behavior.

cards.title: Scaling laws
cards.question: What do scaling laws say, and what changed with Chinchilla?
cards.answer:
• Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data, and compute.
• Kaplan et al. (2020) suggested scaling parameters faster than data. Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) found compute-optimal training scales them roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter.
• In practice models are often trained past Chinchilla-optimal because inference cost depends on model size, so a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve (LLaMA: a 7B model kept improving after 1T tokens, versus Chinchilla's 10B on 200B).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Emergent abilities may partly be an artifact of discontinuous metrics; smooth metrics show smoother improvement.

cards.title: Fine-tuning and LoRA
cards.question: How does LoRA work? When fine-tune vs prompt vs RAG?
cards.answer:
• LoRA: freeze W, learn a low-rank update delta W = B A with rank r much smaller than d. B starts at zero so training starts at the base model. Scale by alpha / r. Trainable parameters drop by orders of magnitude; adapters can be swapped at serve time.
• QLoRA: LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base model.
• Prompting: fastest, no training. RAG: fresh or private knowledge, updated by swapping the index, with inspectable sources. Fine-tuning: change behavior (e.g. instruction following) and how the model uses knowledge it already has.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts: examples with new knowledge are learned slowly and, once learned, increase hallucination; models mostly get facts from pretraining.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.question: Walk through the RLHF pipeline and its failure modes.
cards.answer:
• SFT on demonstrations, then a reward model trained on pairwise human preferences (Bradley-Terry: P(a preferred over b) = sigmoid(r(a) - r(b))), then optimize the policy with PPO against the reward minus a KL penalty to the SFT reference.
• The KL penalty keeps the policy near the reference, where the reward model is accurate, preventing it from exploiting reward-model errors and from collapsing onto a single high-reward answer.
• Failure modes: reward hacking (over-optimizing the reward model), sycophancy, verbosity bias, mode collapse and lost diversity.
cards.key_concept: Probe — RLAIF and Constitutional AI (Anthropic) replace some human labels with AI feedback guided by written principles.

cards.title: DPO
cards.question: What is DPO and how does it differ from PPO-based RLHF?
cards.answer:
• Direct Preference Optimization skips the explicit reward model and RL loop. Loss: -log sigmoid(beta * [log(pi(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)) - log(pi(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x))]).
• Simpler and more stable; offline on a fixed preference dataset, with no sampling from the model during training.
• Tradeoffs: no online exploration; the paper leaves open how it generalizes out of distribution versus an explicit reward model, how reward over-optimization shows up, and how it scales beyond 6B.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Beta plays the role of the KL penalty strength.

cards.title: Decoding strategies
cards.question: Greedy, beam search, temperature, top-k, top-p.
cards.answer:
• Greedy: argmax each step; repetitive. Beam: keeps top b sequences; good for translation, bland for open-ended text.
• Temperature: divide logits by T; lower is sharper, higher is more diverse.
• Top-k: sample from the k most likely. Top-p (nucleus): sample from the smallest set whose probability sums to p, so it adapts to confidence.
cards.key_concept: Probe — For evals, sample multiple times at nonzero temperature and estimate from many samples (Codex draws n = 200 per task because a single draw gives a high-variance estimate), or you mistake noise for improvement.

cards.title: KV cache
cards.question: What is cached, and how big is it?
cards.answer:
• Keys and values of past tokens at every layer, so each new token only computes its own Q, K, V.
• Memory ≈ 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x seq_len x batch x bytes per value.
• Example: 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, 32k tokens, bf16: 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 32768 x 2 bytes ≈ 10.7 GB per sequence.
cards.key_concept: Probe — KV cache, not weights, often caps batch size and therefore throughput. Fixes: GQA, KV quantization, paging, prefix caching.

cards.title: Prefill vs decode
cards.question: Why are prefill and decode different, and what metrics do you track?
cards.answer:
• Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel: compute-bound.
• Decode generates one token at a time, rereading all weights and the KV cache per step: memory-bandwidth-bound.
• Metrics: time to first token (prefill-driven), time per output token or inter-token latency (decode-driven), throughput in tokens per second, cost per query or per token, and tail percentiles (such as p90) of each latency.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate pools because they want different hardware tradeoffs.

cards.title: Continuous batching and PagedAttention
cards.question: How do these raise serving throughput?
cards.answer:
• Static batching waits for the longest sequence. Continuous (in-flight) batching adds and removes requests at every decode step, keeping the GPU full.
• PagedAttention (vLLM): stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks like virtual memory pages, eliminating external fragmentation, keeping internal waste near zero, and enabling sharing of common prefixes.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Prefix caching reuses the KV cache for shared system prompts, cutting time to first token and cost.

cards.title: Speculative decoding
cards.question: How does it work and why is it lossless?
cards.answer:
• A cheap draft model proposes k tokens; the big model verifies all k in one parallel forward pass.
• Accept tokens with a rejection-sampling rule that provably preserves the target model's distribution; on rejection, resample from the corrected distribution.
• Speedup depends on acceptance rate; it trades extra compute for fewer sequential steps, which helps because decode is bandwidth-bound.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Variants: self-speculation with extra decoding heads instead of a separate draft model (Medusa); near-free n-gram table-lookup drafts (even a bigram draft gave a 1.25x speedup in the original paper).

cards.title: Quantization
cards.question: What gets quantized, and what are the tradeoffs?
cards.answer:
• Weight-only (int8, int4 via GPTQ or AWQ) cuts memory and bandwidth, which speeds decode. Activation quantization (int8) speeds compute-bound matrix multiplies but outliers make it harder.
• KV cache quantization raises max batch size.
• Tradeoff: quality loss grows at lower bits and hits small models harder. Evaluate on your own tasks, not just perplexity.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Outlier features in activations are why naive int8 failed; methods like SmoothQuant shift difficulty from activations into weights.

cards.title: Mixture of Experts
cards.question: How do MoE models work, and what are the systems tradeoffs?
cards.answer:
• Replace the MLP with many experts; a router picks the top-k experts per token. Total parameters are large, active parameters per token are small.
• Needs a load-balancing loss so tokens spread evenly across experts; experts with too many tokens overflow and drop them.
• Systems: all parameters must be in memory; expert parallelism requires all-to-all communication; each expert sees only about tokens / num_experts of a batch, so batching is less efficient at low traffic.
cards.key_concept: Probe — MoE lowers FLOPs per token but not memory, so it helps compute-bound settings more than memory-bound small-batch serving.

cards.title: RAG
cards.question: Design a RAG pipeline and name its failure modes.
cards.answer:
• Ingest and chunk documents, embed, store in a vector index (optionally hybrid with BM25, fusing the rankings), retrieve top-k, rerank with a cross-encoder that scores each query-document pair, put in the prompt, generate with citations.
• Failure modes: bad chunking splits answers, retrieval misses (recall problem), extra or irrelevant context goes unused or distracts the model, the model ignores context or hallucinates beyond it, stale index.
• Evaluate separately: retrieval recall@k and MRR, then answer faithfulness and correctness.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Long-context models do not remove RAG: cost, latency, and freshness, plus accuracy drops for information in the middle of long contexts.

cards.title: LLM evaluation
cards.question: How do you evaluate an LLM or an LLM product, and what are the pitfalls?
cards.answer:
• Layers: static benchmarks, hand-written task-specific test sets, LLM-as-judge (pairwise or single-answer grading), human evaluation (the gold standard, but slow and costly), and live crowdsourced comparisons with real users.
• Pitfalls: benchmark contamination; LLM-judge biases (position, verbosity, possibly self-preference), so swap answer order, use pairwise comparisons, calibrate against humans; small eval sets give noisy results.
• Code: pass@k (probability at least one of k samples passes the tests).
• Report confidence intervals; run multiple seeds and samples.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How do you know your judge is good? Measure agreement with expert human labels on a held-out set, and track it over time.

cards.title: Hallucination
cards.question: Why do LLMs hallucinate, and how do you reduce it?
cards.answer:
• The objective rewards plausible continuations, not truth; rare facts are poorly learned; training and evaluation can reward confident guesses over abstaining.
• Mitigations: retrieval grounding with citations, training to abstain or express uncertainty, verification steps, constrained decoding for structured outputs, evals that score "I don't know" correctly.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How do you measure it? Factuality evals on questions with known answers, citation-faithfulness checks, and calibration of stated confidence.

cards.title: Interpretability and safety evaluation (Anthropic emphasis)
cards.question: What is superposition, how do sparse autoencoders help, and what do safety evals look at?
cards.answer:
• Superposition: models represent more features than they have dimensions by packing them in nearly orthogonal directions, so individual neurons are polysemantic.
• Sparse autoencoders (dictionary learning) decompose activations into many sparse, more interpretable features.
• Safety evals: red-teaming, jailbreak robustness, dangerous-capability evals, honesty and sycophancy evals, behavior under distribution shift.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why does this matter to an MLE, not just researchers? You may build the eval infrastructure, data pipelines, and monitoring that these depend on; read Anthropic's published work before an interview there.

cards.title: Accuracy on imbalanced data
cards.question: Fraud is 0.1% of transactions. Why is accuracy a bad metric?
cards.answer: • Predicting "not fraud" always gives 99.9% accuracy and catches nothing.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What single number would you report instead? Recall at a fixed precision (or fixed review capacity), plus PR-AUC.

cards.title: Precision and recall
cards.question: Formulas and one-line intuitions.
cards.answer:
• Precision = TP / (TP + FP): trust in an alarm.
• Recall = TP / (TP + FN): share of actual positives caught.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Which one does the base rate hit hardest? Precision (STAT-01).

cards.title: Recall vs precision for fraud
cards.question: Which do you lean toward, and what is the failure mode?
cards.answer:
• Usually recall, because a missed fraud costs the whole transaction amount (the bank is liable).
• Failure mode: refusing legitimate transactions has a real cost too (it annoys customers), so too many false positives backfire.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Frame it as an expected-cost threshold (FRD-05), not a slogan.

cards.title: F1 and F-beta
cards.question: What does F-beta do?
cards.answer: • F1: harmonic mean of precision and recall. F-beta: beta greater than 1 favors recall.
cards.key_concept: Probe — F-scores ignore true negatives and assume a fixed threshold; for business decisions, a cost matrix is more honest.

cards.title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
cards.question: Which curve for a 0.1% positive class, and why?
cards.answer:
• ROC: TPR vs FPR. FPR's denominator is the huge negative pool, so many false positives barely move it, and ROC-AUC looks great while precision is terrible.
• PR curve: precision vs recall; sensitive to how the model handles the rare class. Use it to choose thresholds.
cards.key_concept: Probe — PR-AUC's baseline is the positive rate (0.001), not 0.5, so compare against that.

cards.title: Metrics by domain
cards.question: Core metrics for ranking, ad CTR, A/B testing, and forecasting.
cards.answer:
• Ranking: Precision@K, Recall@K, NDCG, MRR, MAP.
• Ad CTR: log loss or normalized entropy, calibration, per-user (impression-weighted) AUC.
• A/B: significance, confidence intervals, power, minimum detectable effect, peeking, guardrails.
• Forecasting: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why does MAPE misbehave? It is infinite or undefined when an actual is zero, extreme near zero, and penalizes negative errors (over-forecasts, since e = y − ŷ) more than positive ones; scaled errors such as MASE avoid dividing by the actuals.

cards.title: What AUC means
cards.question: Give the probabilistic interpretation of ROC-AUC and what it does not tell you.
cards.answer:
• The probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative. Threshold-free; only the ranking matters.
• Does not measure calibration, and a global AUC mixes inter-user and intra-user order, so it can hide poor ranking within each user (what matters for feeds and ads).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Use per-user AUC (GAUC): AUC per user, averaged with impression weights; DIN reports it tracks online performance better in display ads.

cards.title: NDCG
cards.question: Write DCG and NDCG. Why the log discount?
cards.answer:
• DCG@K = sum over i = 1..K of (2^rel_i - 1) / log2(i + 1).
• NDCG@K = DCG@K / IDCG@K, where IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ordering. Ranges from 0 to 1.
• The log discount gives higher-ranked results more weight (position dependence for what the user sees); graded relevance rewards putting the best items first.
cards.key_concept: Probe — NDCG uses graded relevance labels (MRR and MAP are designed for binary relevance); with implicit feedback you derive grades from signals (click 1, long watch 2, purchase 3), which is a modeling choice you should defend.

cards.title: Retrieval-stage vs ranking-stage metrics
cards.question: Which metrics fit candidate generation vs final ranking?
cards.answer:
• Candidate generation: Recall@K (did the good items make it into the few hundred candidates?); ordering matters little.
• Ranking: NDCG@K, MAP, MRR (order matters, top positions dominate).
cards.key_concept: Probe — A ranker cannot recover items the retriever dropped, so retrieval recall upper-bounds final quality.

cards.title: Log loss and normalized entropy
cards.question: Why is log loss the main offline metric for CTR models, and what is normalized entropy?
cards.answer:
• CTR feeds auctions and value models, so you need calibrated probabilities; log loss rewards both ranking and calibration.
• Normalized entropy (Facebook) = model log loss / log loss of always predicting the average CTR. Lower is better; it makes results comparable across datasets with different base rates.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How big an improvement matters? At ad scale small offline gains count: Facebook says a typical feature-engineering experiment shaves off a couple of tens of a percent of relative NE; the DCN paper treats a 0.001 log-loss gain on Criteo as practically significant; Wide & Deep's slightly higher offline AUC (0.728 vs 0.726) came with a +3.9% online acquisition gain. Say which holdout and what confidence interval you would need before believing it.

cards.title: Offline-online gap
cards.question: Your offline NDCG went up but the A/B test is flat. Why, and what do you do?
cards.answer:
• Logged data only shows what the old system chose (selection bias); offline metrics fit past engagement and miss long-term effects; the metric does not match the business objective (local wins that do not move retention); training-serving skew; position bias in labels.
• Tools: counterfactual or off-policy evaluation with inverse propensity scoring (needs logged propensities, high variance), interleaving for fast ranker comparisons, better proxy metrics correlated with long-term outcomes.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Log propensities (the probability the old policy showed each item) at serving time; IPS needs them (or estimates from randomized interventions), and the old policy must give every item a nonzero chance.

cards.title: Beyond-accuracy recommendation metrics
cards.question: What should you measure besides relevance?
cards.answer:
• Diversity (intra-list dissimilarity), novelty, catalog coverage, serendipity, freshness.
• Long-term: retention, churn. Netflix framing: optimize medium-term engagement and member retention, not just clicks.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Optimizing clicks can promote clickbait (YouTube ranks by expected watch time instead), and many local engagement wins never move retention; check long-term metrics.

cards.title: Designing an A/B test
cards.question: Walk through designing an A/B test for a new ranking model, including sample size.
cards.answer:
• Hypothesis; randomization unit (usually user); primary metric (OEC); guardrails (for example crashes, latency); duration in whole weeks to cover day-of-week effects.
• Sample size (Kohavi et al. 2007): total n ≈ (4 r sigma / delta)^2 for 95% confidence and 90% power, with r variants and delta the minimum difference to detect, so about 32 sigma^2 / delta^2 per arm for an A/B test (the authors note it may overestimate by about 25% for large n).
• Decide the OEC and stopping rule in advance.
cards.key_concept: Probe — If the required sample is too large, reduce variance (EXP-03, or analyze only users who could see the change), choose a lower-variance metric, or use interleaving (EXP-07).

cards.title: Peeking and sequential testing
cards.question: Why is checking results daily and stopping at significance a problem?
cards.answer:
• Each look is another chance for a false positive; continuous monitoring inflates type I error far above alpha (Johari et al.: fivefold even at 10,000 samples).
• Fixes: fixed horizon, sequential tests (as in clinical trials), always-valid inference (mSPRT).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Always-valid p-values keep type I error controlled at any data-dependent stopping time, so you can stop early when a true effect shows or give up sooner; auto-aborting a significantly underperforming treatment limits harm.

cards.title: CUPED
cards.question: How does CUPED reduce variance?
cards.answer:
• Use a pre-experiment covariate X (often the same metric before the test): Y_adj = Y - theta * (X - mean(X)), theta = cov(Y, X) / var(X).
• Unbiased because X is independent of treatment; the variance is multiplied by (1 - rho^2), where rho is the correlation between X and Y. A correlation of 0.7 roughly halves it.
cards.key_concept: Probe — New users have no pre-period data; use other covariates or accept less reduction for them.

cards.title: Interference and network effects
cards.question: When does user-level randomization break?
cards.answer:
• When treatment of one unit affects others (violates SUTVA): two-sided marketplaces (buyers compete for shared supply or budgets, e.g. ads), social networks (users interact with their connections), ride-hailing.
• Fixes: cluster randomization (network clusters, country-level), switchback experiments (alternate the whole market between treatment and control over time), budget-split designs for ads.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Each fix has its own assumption: cluster randomization is unbiased only if clusters do not interfere with each other, and switchbacks only if there is no carryover between periods.

cards.title: Novelty, primacy, and long-term effects
cards.question: Why can early A/B results mislead?
cards.answer:
• Novelty: users explore anything new, then the effect fades. Primacy: experienced users do worse at first with a changed design (change aversion).
• Run for multiple weeks and watch the effect over time, compare new vs returning users (new users have neither bias), run longer experiments.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Surrogate metrics (short-term signals shown to predict long-term retention, like Netflix's engagement) let you decide sooner.

cards.title: Sample ratio mismatch
cards.question: You planned 50/50 but got 50.6/49.4 with millions of users. What now?
cards.answer:
• Run a chi-square test; with millions of users that gap is highly significant (Fabijan et al.: even 50.2/49.8 on about 1.6M users has under a 1 in 500k chance), so assignment or logging is broken (bot filtering, redirects, crashes in one arm, caching).
• Do not trust any metric until fixed.
cards.key_concept: Probe — SRM is a standard automated data-quality check on experimentation platforms; about 6% of Microsoft experiments show one.

cards.title: Interleaving
cards.question: What is interleaving and why does Netflix use it for ranking?
cards.answer:
• Merge results from rankers A and B into one list per user (for example team-draft) and credit the ranker whose items get clicked.
• Each user compares both directly (a paired comparison); in Chapelle et al. interleaving needed over an order of magnitude fewer queries than an absolute click metric.
• Netflix (2015) was exploring interleaving-based tests as a faster, more predictive replacement for offline experiments when choosing which algorithms go to full A/B tests on streaming and retention.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Interleaving says which ranker users prefer, not the size of the effect on retention or revenue; Netflix noted it was still unclear when interleaving results track retention wins.

cards.title: Ratio metrics and the delta method
cards.question: You randomize by user but measure CTR as clicks / impressions. What is wrong with a naive t-test?
cards.answer:
• Impressions from the same user are correlated, so treating them as independent understates variance and inflates false positives.
• Use the delta method to get the variance of a ratio of user-level sums, or bootstrap (much costlier at scale).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Rule: the analysis unit must match the randomization unit, or you must correct for it.

cards.title: Training-serving skew
cards.question: What causes training-serving skew and how do you prevent it?
cards.answer:
• Different code paths or preprocessing for features offline vs online; feature tables that change between training and serving time (a join sees different values); upstream input signals that change behavior; feedback loops between the model and the system.
• Prevent: re-use code between training and serving, or one feature definition shared by both paths (feature store); log the features actually served and train on those logs; monitor skew explicitly.
cards.key_concept: Probe — "Log and wait" (training on served features) removes skew, but a new feature has no logged history until it has been served for a while; if you cannot log every example, log a small fraction to verify training/serving consistency.

cards.title: Point-in-time correctness
cards.question: What does a feature store's point-in-time join guarantee?
cards.answer:
• For each training example at time t, the join scans backward from t (up to a TTL) and takes the latest feature value at or before t, never later values. Prevents temporal leakage.
• Feature stores also provide batch access for training, low-latency online serving, and standardized shared feature definitions.
cards.key_concept: Probe — By default Feast's join constrains only the feature's event timestamp, so values backfilled or corrected later can still leak into training; filtering on created timestamp <= example timestamp reproduces what the online store would have served.

cards.title: Negative sampling and logQ correction
cards.question: With implicit feedback, where do negatives come from, and what bias does in-batch sampling create?
cards.answer:
• Options: negatives sampled from a background distribution with an importance-weighting correction (candidate sampling, YouTube DNN), in-batch items (other examples' positives), impressed-but-not-engaged items (exist only for what the old system chose to show).
• In-batch items follow a power-law (popularity) distribution, so popular items get over-penalized as negatives.
• logQ correction: subtract log(sampling probability) of each item from its logit during training (Yi et al. 2019, YouTube).
cards.key_concept: Probe — In streaming data the item vocabulary keeps changing, so Yi et al. estimate each item's sampling probability online with hash arrays, adapting to distribution change.

cards.title: Delayed labels
cards.question: Conversions arrive up to 30 days after a click; chargebacks months after a transaction. How do you train?
cards.answer:
• Waiting for mature labels makes training data stale, and accuracy degrades as the gap between training and test data grows; labeling too early mislabels late positives as negatives and biases the positive rate low.
• Fixed waiting window (Facebook ads online joiner): an impression becomes a negative only if no click arrives within a tuned window. Too long delays training data and needs more memory to buffer impressions; too short loses positives. The residual bias can be measured and corrected.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Quantify the cost of waiting: Facebook found normalized entropy improves about 1% going from weekly to daily retraining, so staleness costs real accuracy.

cards.title: High-cardinality categoricals
cards.question: Options for a feature with millions of values, and the leakage risk in target encoding.
cards.answer:
• One-hot (inflates the feature space at high cardinality), hashing into a fixed-size vector (bounded memory; rare tokens still contribute), learned embeddings, target encoding.
• Target encoding uses the label mean per category, so compute it with cross fitting (each fold encoded from the other folds) plus smoothing toward the global mean, or target information leaks into training.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Rare categories: shrink toward the global mean (more shrinkage for small counts), or group them into an "infrequent" bucket; unseen categories get the global target mean.

cards.title: Labeling strategy
cards.question: You need labels for harmful content at scale. How do you get them?
cards.answer:
• Human raters with detailed labeling instructions, screened on agreement with researcher labels for sensitive content; subject-matter experts for hard policies (expensive).
• Active learning: estimate which examples are most useful to label, reducing manual annotation.
• Weak supervision: patterns, heuristics and crowd labels written as labeling functions, combined by a generative model that learns their accuracies from their agreements and disagreements without ground truth (Snorkel). AI feedback guided by written principles can replace human harm labels (Constitutional AI).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Measure label quality with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa; above 0.8 is generally good agreement) and audit sets; weak sources have limited accuracy and coverage, so pass label-quality information (probabilistic labels) to the end model.

cards.title: Exploration vs exploitation
cards.question: Define both, and compare epsilon-greedy, UCB, and Thompson sampling.
cards.answer:
• Exploitation: choose what the model currently believes is best. Exploration: try seemingly suboptimal options to learn more about them.
• Epsilon-greedy: random action with probability epsilon (0.05 = 95/5). Simple but explores blindly (uniformly at random).
• UCB: pick the highest estimated mean plus a confidence-interval bonus; total regret only logarithmic in the number of trials (context-free case).
• Thompson sampling: sample from each option's posterior and pick the best sample; each option is chosen with the probability that it is optimal given the history.
• Contextual bandits condition on user and item features (LinUCB for Yahoo! news recommendation) and generalize to new users and items.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Exploration raises short-term regret to lower long-term regret; quantify the cost as regret and cap it with a traffic budget (a small slice of traffic for exploration).

cards.title: Multi-stage architecture
cards.question: Why do large recommenders use multiple stages? Sketch them with rough sizes.
cards.answer:
• Corpus of millions under a strict serving latency (YouTube: scoring millions of items within tens of milliseconds needs a sublinear scheme), so cheap models first, expensive later.
• Candidate generation from multiple sources (learned embeddings with nearest-neighbor search, co-watch counts, topic matching) narrows millions to hundreds; a heavier ranker with richer features scores those hundreds and presents dozens. A re-ranking pass for diversity can follow (REC-13).
cards.key_concept: Probe — A ranker only works on the candidates it receives, so retrieval must emit highly relevant candidates; train and evaluate each stage knowing what the next stage does.

cards.title: Two-tower model
cards.question: How is a two-tower model trained and served, and what is its main limitation?
cards.answer:
• User tower and item tower each produce an embedding; score = dot product.
• Training: in-batch softmax with logQ correction (subtract the log of the item's in-batch sampling probability from each logit), or many sampled negatives from a fixed vocabulary.
• Serving: precompute item embeddings offline into an ANN (maximum inner product) index; compute the user embedding online with the query tower and retrieve nearest items.
• Limitation: user and item interact only through the final dot product; interaction-based models that compare query and item features directly tend to be more accurate but cannot precompute item representations. That is the ranker's job.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Indexed item embeddings come from one item-tower version; YouTube's index pipeline periodically recomputes them and ships the query tower stitched together with the index as one serving model.

cards.title: Approximate nearest neighbor search
cards.question: Compare HNSW, IVF, and product quantization.
cards.answer:
• HNSW: hierarchy of proximity graphs, search starts at the sparse top layer; excellent recall and speed; memory-heavy (graph links on top of the raw vectors, far more RAM than PQ); supports incremental inserts, but the original paper leaves element updates and removal to future work.
• IVF: cluster vectors with k-means (coarse quantizer), search only the nearest clusters (nprobe, the number of probed lists, trades recall for speed).
• PQ: split vectors into subvectors and quantize each with its own small k-means codebook (typically 256 centroids, one byte each); huge memory savings, approximate distances computed on the codes. IVF-PQ (IVFADC) is the standard at billion scale.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Measure recall@K of the ANN against exact search on a sample of queries; tune nprobe or ef to the latency budget.

cards.title: Collaborative filtering and matrix factorization
cards.question: How does matrix factorization work for implicit feedback?
cards.answer:
• Approximate the user-item matrix as U V^T; each user and item gets a latent vector and the prediction is their inner product.
• Implicit ALS: binarize to a preference (consumed or not) with confidence c = 1 + alpha * r, so unobserved entries are low-confidence negatives; the loss covers all user-item pairs, and with one side fixed it is quadratic, so alternate closed-form solves for U and V.
• Limits: cold start for new items; MF captures only second-order interactions and does not take general feature vectors, which motivated factorization machines and two-tower models.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Two-tower with only ID features is essentially matrix factorization trained with a softmax loss (YouTube's first neural retrievers mimicked MF with shallow networks over watch-ID embeddings).

cards.title: Cold start
cards.question: Strategies for new users and new items.
cards.answer:
• New users: demographic and context features (region, device, age) as priors, popularity and short-term trending, an onboarding survey (Netflix asks new members to pick videos at sign-up), contextual bandits that generalize across users through features.
• New items: content features (visual, audio) in the item tower, an example-age feature so fresh uploads are not underrated, features about the user's history with the uploading channel, a small exploration traffic slice.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Measure cold start as its own slice: Netflix reports its recommender works well for members with long histories but not for new members, whose cancellation rates are highest.

cards.title: Ranking architectures
cards.question: Wide & Deep, DCN, DLRM, and multi-task models.
cards.answer:
• Wide & Deep: jointly trained linear model on cross-product features (memorization) plus a deep net (generalization).
• DCN: explicit cross layers learn bounded-degree feature interactions efficiently; the highest degree is set by layer depth.
• DLRM: embeddings for sparse features, MLP for dense, dot products between all pairs of embedding vectors, then a top MLP.
• Multi-task: shared bottom or MMoE (experts shared across tasks, a gating network per task) predict click, watch time, like, dismissal together; MMoE reduces the harm hard sharing does when tasks are weakly correlated.
cards.key_concept: Probe — User-history features carry the most signal: YouTube found features describing the user's past interaction with the item and similar items most important, and DIN attends over the user's behaviors with weights that depend on the candidate ad.

cards.title: Multi-objective ranking
cards.question: How do you combine predicted click, watch time, likes, and hides into one ranking score?
cards.answer:
• Value model: predict each behavior (click, watch time, like, dismissal) and combine the predictions into one score with a combination function; YouTube uses a weighted multiplication with manually tuned weights.
• Tune the weights in live A/B tests against both engagement metrics (time spent) and satisfaction metrics (dismissal rate, survey responses).
• Calibrated predictions make the weights meaningful: once predictions feed arithmetic, their accuracy matters, not just their ranking order.
cards.key_concept: Probe — The weights trade engagement against satisfaction; treat weight changes as product decisions checked against satisfaction guardrails, not only engagement wins.

cards.title: Position bias and feedback loops
cards.question: How do position bias and feedback loops corrupt training data, and how do you fix them?
cards.answer:
• Items shown higher get clicked more regardless of relevance. Training on that teaches the model its own past choices (feedback loop, popularity bias).
• Fixes: add position as a training feature and set it to a fixed value at serving; a separate shallow position tower; inverse propensity weighting with estimated examination probabilities; randomized exploration traffic.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Estimate position effects with small randomization experiments (swap adjacent items).

cards.title: Sequential and generative recommenders
cards.question: How do transformers model user histories? What is the generative recommendation idea (HSTU)?
cards.answer:
• SASRec: causal self-attention over the item sequence predicts the next item. BERT4Rec: masked-item prediction, bidirectional.
• Generative recommenders (Meta's HSTU): treat user actions as tokens in a long sequence and train a large sequence model for retrieval and ranking; shows LLM-like scaling with compute.
• Semantic IDs (TIGER-style): represent items as short code sequences so a model can generate item IDs.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Costs: very long user sequences make serving expensive; you need caching of user-state encodings and efficient attention.

cards.title: YouTube DNN paper
cards.question: Key ideas from "Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations" (2016).
cards.answer:
• Candidate generation as extreme multiclass classification with sampled softmax; serving via nearest neighbor search on the learned embeddings.
• "Example age" feature lets the model learn freshness preferences and remove a bias toward old content.
• Ranking with weighted logistic regression: positives weighted by watch time so the odds approximate expected watch time.
• Predict the next watch rather than a randomly held-out watch, which respects asymmetric consumption patterns.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why watch time, not CTR? CTR promotes deceptive videos users do not finish (clickbait); watch time better captures engagement.

cards.title: Netflix-flavored problems
cards.question: What makes recommendations at Netflix different, and what techniques fit?
cards.answer:
• Subscription business: revenue comes only from the monthly fee and members can cancel any time, so the main target is member retention, not ad impressions; engagement (time spent viewing) correlates strongly with retention and is the practical A/B metric.
• Page construction: choosing and ordering rows (about 40 per homepage) for relevance and diversity, not just ranking a single list.
• Evidence selection, including which artwork image to show for each title; interleaving explored for faster local-metric tests; A/B tests running 2 to 6 months, preferably on new members.
• Mixed content length: counting hours over-credits multi-season shows, counting distinct titles over-credits movies.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How do you get a training signal for retention, which is slow and sparse? Engagement metrics that correlate with retention, checked in long A/B tests; detecting a 0.1% retention change needs roughly 2 million members per cell.

cards.title: Re-ranking and diversity
cards.question: How do you add diversity without killing relevance?
cards.answer:
• Maximal Marginal Relevance: greedily pick the item that is both relevant and least similar to items already picked, scoring lambda * relevance - (1 - lambda) * similarity to the picked set; lambda = 1 gives the plain relevance ranking, lambda = 0 maximal diversity.
• Determinantal point processes: probabilistic models of repulsion that give higher probability to diverse sets.
• Page level: Netflix selects and orders whole rows to optimize relevance and diversity together.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why diversify? Moods change between sessions and accounts are shared, so a diverse page lets a member skip what suits another time or person; Netflix's relevance-and-diversity page algorithm beat a template page in A/B tests.

cards.title: Ad ranking and auctions
cards.question: How are ads ranked, and why must pCTR be calibrated?
cards.answer:
• Expected value per impression ≈ bid x pCTR (x pCVR for conversion bids); Google ranks ads by bid x quality score, a score based on CTR and other factors (originally just the estimated CTR).
• Generalized second-price auction: each advertiser pays the smallest amount sufficient to keep its rank above the next advertiser (with equal quality: the next bid plus an increment).
• The probability is multiplied by money, so miscalibration directly misprices ads and misallocates budget; ranking quality alone is not enough.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Overpredicting pCTR for one advertiser segment inflates its rank score, so it wins slots it should lose (and, since its GSP price per click is the next rank score divided by its own quality score, pays less per click), costing revenue and crowding out better ads. Monitor calibration by segment.

cards.title: Feature interactions for CTR
cards.question: FM, FFM, and why crosses matter.
cards.answer:
• CTR depends on interactions (user segment x ad category x time). Manually adding pairwise crosses to a linear model does not scale to many features and cannot generalize to pairs rarely or never seen in training.
• Factorization machines: model every pairwise interaction as the dot product of learned latent vectors, so sparse crosses still generalize.
• FFM: each feature has one latent vector per field and uses the one matching the other feature's field; stronger, more parameters (n x f x k instead of n x k).
• Deep successors: DeepFM, DCN, DLRM.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Embedding tables for ad and user IDs hold most of the parameters (several tables of multiple GBs each), so they are sharded across devices with model parallelism while the MLPs use data parallelism; that drives system design.

cards.title: Negative downsampling correction
cards.question: You keep all clicks but only 10% of non-clicks. How do you fix predicted probabilities?
cards.answer:
• With negative sampling rate w (0.1), the model's p is inflated. Corrected q = p / (p + (1 - p) / w).
• Equivalent: add log(w) to the logit.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Verify with the calibration ratio on unsampled holdout traffic.

cards.title: Freshness and continual training
cards.question: Why do ads models retrain continuously, and what are the risks?
cards.answer:
• Click-prediction data distributions change over time: Facebook found accuracy degrades day by day after training, and moving from weekly to daily retraining cut NE by about 1%.
• Online learning: a real-time joiner labels impressions with clicks and the trainer learns continuously, publishing new models periodically (boosted trees retrained daily, the linear layer near real time).
• Risks: bad data corrupts the model quickly (a stale click stream yields near-zero CTR predictions and fewer ads shown); delayed labels force a waiting window (DATA-04).
• Safeguards: anomaly detection that disconnects the online trainer when the training data distribution changes abruptly; track NE and calibration.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How long to wait before labeling an impression a non-click? Too long delays training data and costs buffer memory; too short loses clicks and biases empirical CTR low (a small bias that can be measured and corrected).

cards.title: Evaluating a CTR model
cards.question: Which offline and online metrics?
cards.answer:
• Offline: normalized entropy (log loss divided by the entropy of the background CTR), calibration ratio (expected over observed clicks; also check it by segment), AUC (ranking quality only, blind to calibration).
• Online: CTR, value delivered to advertisers, and revenue received by the marketplace operator.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Budgets make A/B arms interfere: with finite budgets, treatment gains cannibalize control and the effect is overestimated. Budget-split experiments randomly split members into two buckets and split each campaign's budget in proportion.

cards.title: BM25
cards.question: What does BM25 score, and what do its parameters do?
cards.answer:
• Sum over query terms of IDF(term) x tf / (tf + k1 (1 - b + b x doc_len / avg_len)). Many implementations also multiply by (k1 + 1), a constant that does not change the ranking.
• IDF rewards rare terms; k1 saturates term frequency so repetition gives diminishing returns up to a cap; b normalizes for document length (b = 1 full normalization, b = 0 none). Typical values: k1 between 1.2 and 2, b between 0.5 and 0.8.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why keep BM25 alongside dense retrieval? Exact term matching, including rare words that fixed embedding vocabularies miss, and it is a cheap first stage (MS MARCO neural re-rankers work on BM25's top 1000).

cards.title: Bi-encoders, cross-encoders, hybrid
cards.question: Tradeoffs between bi-encoders and cross-encoders, and how do you fuse lexical and dense results?
cards.answer:
• Bi-encoder: query and document embedded separately; document embeddings precomputed offline; fast sublinear (ANN) retrieval; less accurate than interaction-based models.
• Cross-encoder: query and document together through one transformer; more accurate, but BERT rankers cost 100 to 1000x more than earlier models, so use it to rerank a candidate set (MS MARCO setup: BM25's top 1000).
• Hybrid fusion: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, score = sum of 1 / (k + rank) across retrievers (k = 60, near-optimal but not critical), or a learned combination.
cards.key_concept: Probe — ColBERT-style late interaction sits between them: per-token embeddings for query and document, document side precomputed, relevance = sum over query tokens of the max similarity to any document token (MaxSim).

cards.title: Learning to rank
cards.question: Pointwise vs pairwise vs listwise. What is LambdaMART?
cards.answer:
• Pointwise: predict a relevance score per document (regression or classification).
• Pairwise: learn which of two documents should rank higher (RankNet: sigmoid of the score difference, cross-entropy loss).
• Listwise: learn from the ordering of the whole list, or optimize a list-level metric directly.
• LambdaMART: gradient-boosted trees (MART) trained on lambda gradients, the RankNet pairwise gradients multiplied by the change in NDCG from swapping the pair. A strong classic baseline: a LambdaMART ensemble won Track 1 of the 2010 Yahoo! Learning to Rank Challenge.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Labels: expert relevance judgments (expensive, often infeasible) vs click logs (cheap but biased by presentation order, REC-09).

cards.title: Query understanding and search evaluation
cards.question: What happens to a query before retrieval, and how do you evaluate search?
cards.answer:
• Inferring intent before retrieval: stemming and lemmatization, query segmentation (e.g. New York as one unit), entity recognition, spelling correction, query rewriting (expansion and relaxation raise recall; phrasing and field restriction raise precision).
• Offline: NDCG and MRR on human-judged query sets. Online: click-through rate, session success rate, session abandonment rate, zero-result rate.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Zero-result queries are their own failure slice: they signal a recall problem or content missing from the index; track them and fix recall with expansion or relaxation.

cards.title: Visual and multimodal search
cards.question: How would you build image search ("find similar") and text-to-video search?
cards.answer:
• Visual: embed images with a deep network (Pinterest: CNN activations; CLIP: a contrastively trained image encoder); nearest-neighbor index; rerank the top candidates with extra signals such as text annotations; optionally detect the object of interest first and embed its bounding box.
• Text-to-video: CLIP-style joint text-image embeddings applied to video frames, plus a lexical token index on text metadata alongside the visual index.
