• Train with a contrastive loss on paired data: CLIP maximizes similarity for the N true pairs in a batch and minimizes it for the N^2 - N wrong pairings; engagement pairs (query, clicked result) are the in-house analogue.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Video is long: a single image is far from enough to encode a video; embed frames and aggregate (CLIP4Clip: mean pooling for small datasets, a temporal self-attention layer for large ones), or index segments so results can jump to a timestamp.

cards.title: Fraud system design essentials
cards.question: What makes fraud detection different from typical classification?
cards.answer:
• Adversaries adapt: fraudsters adopt new techniques as old ones are fixed (concept drift), made worse by delayed fraud reporting; labels are incomplete (investigators can check only a few alerts per day); extreme imbalance (typically well under 1% fraud); asymmetric costs; real-time latency (blocking rules run within milliseconds, before authorization; scoring may get tens of milliseconds).
• Typical stack: terminal checks and transaction-blocking rules in real time, then scoring rules and an ML score in near real time, then human investigators whose verdicts feed back as labels.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Rules are not a legacy embarrassment: investigators write fast, very precise blocking rules for known patterns. But scoring rules only catch strategies investigators already found, are subjective and hard to maintain; the model finds patterns beyond investigator experience.

cards.title: Graph signals
cards.question: How do graph features help catch fraud rings?
cards.answer:
• Attackers have limited devices and time, so their accounts sign up or log in on a small number of shared devices (device aggregation) and burst in a short window (activity aggregation). Build an account-device graph (phone number, MAC, IMEI, SIM); features like connected component size and node degree feed a classifier such as GBDT.
• Graph neural networks learn from each account's neighborhood end to end (GEM at Alipay). Shared links are noisy: normal accounts share IPs with malicious ones through common proxies.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Graph features are costly to compute in real time: GEM rebuilds the graph daily from the past 7 days of account-device activity and leaves real-time detection on dynamic graphs to future work.

cards.title: Unsupervised anomaly detection
cards.question: When labels are scarce, what can you use?
cards.answer:
• Isolation forest: anomalies are few and different, so random partitioning isolates them in shorter paths.
• Autoencoders: trained to reconstruct mostly normal data, so high reconstruction error means unusual.
• Density or distance methods (Local Outlier Factor compares a point's local density with that of its k nearest neighbors).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Anomalous is not the same as fraudulent: some fraud patterns are not rare and need supervised learning, and unsupervised scores are less accurate than supervised models. Use anomaly scores as an extra feature for a supervised model or to prioritize review, then learn from reviewer labels.

cards.title: Harmful content detection
cards.question: Design considerations for a harmful content classifier on posts with text, images, and video.
cards.answer:
• Multimodal fusion: late fusion (separate unimodal models, average their scores) is simplest; early fusion (joint model) captures cross-modal meaning (harmless caption plus harmless image that together are mean). On Hateful Memes, early fusion broadly outperformed middle and late fusion.
• Multi-task heads per policy (violence, hate, nudity, spam) sharing a backbone (shared-bottom); if policies conflict, per-task gating (MMoE) reduces the interference.
• Operating point per policy; route uncertain cases to human review, whose decisions become labels; reviewer capacity is limited.
• Metrics: precision and recall at the operating point, prevalence (share of content views that are violating), reviewer load.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Prevalence samples content views, not posts (a post seen 1 million times is 1 million times more likely to be sampled), so it captures what users actually see, including violating content that was never detected or reported.

cards.title: Cost-based thresholds
cards.question: How do you set the decision threshold from business costs?
cards.answer:
• Flag if p x cost_of_miss > (1 - p) x cost_of_false_alarm, so threshold p* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN). Requires calibrated p.
• Add constraints like review capacity: take the top k by score per day (precision top-k).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Costs vary per transaction (amount at risk), so the threshold can vary per transaction too.

cards.title: Drift
cards.question: Covariate shift vs label shift vs concept drift. How do you detect each?
cards.answer:
• Covariate shift: P(x) changes, P(y | x) stays. Label (prior) shift: P(y) changes, P(x | y) stays. Concept drift: P(y | x) changes (fraudsters adapt). Some authors use "concept drift" for any change in P(x, y), calling the P(y | x) case actual drift and the P(x)-only case virtual drift.
• Detect: two-sample tests on input features (KS per feature, KL divergence), tests on the model's prediction distribution (black box shift detection, the best detector in Failing Loudly), accuracy on fresh labels.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Pure P(y | x) drift with P(x) unchanged is invisible to input and prediction-distribution monitors, since predictions depend only on x. You need labels, which are often delayed; a small labeled sample can estimate accuracy.

cards.title: Safe deployment
cards.question: How do you roll out a new model safely?
cards.answer:
• Offline validation gates (beat the current production model, consistent across segments), then shadow mode (a copy of live requests is scored, only production responses are returned, shadow responses are logged for comparison), then canary on a small slice, then A/B test, then gradual (linear) ramp with automatic rollback on alarms.
• Push models to a registry and record pipeline versions and a pointer to the previous model in metadata, so you can roll back.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Shadow mode cannot measure user response (users never see shadow output), only agreement with production, latency, and errors.

cards.title: Batch vs online vs streaming inference
cards.question: When do you use each?
cards.answer:
• Batch (static): precompute predictions on a schedule and cache them (daily recommendations, email); little worry about inference cost and predictions can be verified before serving, but update latency is hours or days and uncommon inputs get no prediction.
• Online (dynamic): compute per request; handles any new or long-tail input; compute intensive and latency sensitive (may force a simpler model), and monitoring is more intensive.
• Streaming: update features or training data from event streams in near real time (session aggregation features, Facebook ads' online joiner).
• Common hybrid: item embeddings computed and indexed periodically, query tower plus nearest-neighbor lookup online, then a separate ranking model (YouTube).
cards.key_concept: Probe — In online serving, adding inference servers does not necessarily fix prediction latency, and on-demand predictions cannot all be verified before use, only monitored in aggregate afterwards.

cards.title: Meeting latency budgets
cards.question: Your ranker is too slow for a 50 ms p99 budget. Options?
cards.answer:
• Distillation to a smaller model suited to deployment; quantization (it cuts latency only with suitable kernels: LLM.int8() saved memory but kept FP16 runtime, GPTQ gave speedups); score fewer candidates behind a cheap candidate-generation stage; precompute and cache what you can.
• Profile first: find which stage (feature fetching, model compute, fan-out) dominates the budget.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Optimize p99, not average: with fan-out, rare slow components dominate (if each server is slow 1 time in 100, 63% of requests that touch 100 servers are slow); hedged requests to replicas cut the tail.

cards.title: Retraining strategy
cards.question: How often should you retrain, and how do you decide?
cards.answer:
• Measure decay: train on one day and evaluate on successively later days to see how fast quality drops.
• Options: scheduled retrains (frequency set by how fast data patterns change and how costly retraining is), trigger on performance degradation or data distribution shift, continuous online training (ads).
• Each retrain needs validation gates and comparison against the current production model.
cards.key_concept: Probe — A model influences the selection of its own future training data (direct feedback loop), which retraining can reinforce; mitigate with some randomization (exploration traffic) or by isolating part of the data from the model.

cards.title: Debugging a production regression
cards.question: Engagement dropped 5% after a model launch. Walk through debugging.
cards.answer:
• Confirm it is real: experiment validity (an SRM, found with a chi-square test, usually invalidates the results), dashboards; compare treatment with control, which balances seasonality and other launches.
• Localize: which segments, platforms, regions; correlate with launch time; compare against holdout.
• Check pipeline: stale inputs, missing or unexpected features (schema skew), training-serving skew, unstable upstream signals, model version actually served.
• Check the model: calibration, score distribution shift, candidate set changes.
• Roll back first if impact is serious, then investigate.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Staff signal: talk about preventing recurrence (a postmortem with root causes and follow-up actions, automated checks, alerts), not just the fix.

cards.title: Data parallelism
cards.question: How does data-parallel training work, and what is ring all-reduce?
cards.answer:
• Each worker holds a full model copy, processes a different shard of the batch, then gradients are averaged across workers.
• Ring all-reduce: workers pass chunks around a ring (reduce-scatter then all-gather); bandwidth per worker stays roughly constant as workers grow.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Overlap gradient communication with the backward pass by bucketing gradients.

cards.title: ZeRO and FSDP
cards.question: What do ZeRO stages 1, 2, 3 shard, and how does PyTorch FSDP relate?
cards.answer:
• Stage 1: optimizer states (4x memory reduction). Stage 2: plus gradients (8x). Stage 3: plus parameters, broadcast partition by partition just in time in the forward pass (and again in backward), then discarded.
• Stages 1 and 2 keep the same communication volume as plain data parallelism; stage 3 makes memory per GPU fall linearly with the number of GPUs for about 50% more communication.
• PyTorch FSDP is motivated by ZeRO: it splits the model into units, shards each unit's parameters, gathers them on demand before computation and discards them right after. Its sharding factor F runs from 1 (plain data parallelism) to the number of GPUs (full sharding); values in between are hybrid sharding (sharded within a group, replicated across groups).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Offloading model states to CPU memory extends this further at the cost of speed: PCI-E bandwidth is limited and up to 50% of training time can go to GPU-CPU-GPU transfers.

cards.title: Tensor and pipeline parallelism
cards.question: When do you need them, and what are their costs?
cards.answer:
• Tensor parallelism: split individual matrix multiplies across GPUs (Megatron: one all-reduce in the forward and one in the backward pass per MLP block); Megatron kept it to 8-way, inside a DGX-2H server (300 GB/s NVSwitch between GPUs vs 100 GB/s between servers).
• Pipeline parallelism: split layers into stages across devices; micro-batches let stages work simultaneously and shrink idle "bubbles" (negligible in GPipe when micro-batches >= 4 x stages).
• 3D parallelism combines data, tensor, and pipeline; add expert parallelism for MoE and sequence parallelism to cut activation memory.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Pipeline bubble fraction is roughly (stages - 1) / (micro-batches + stages - 1), so more micro-batches shrink it.

cards.title: Training memory accounting
cards.question: Estimate memory to train a 7B model with Adam in mixed precision.
cards.answer:
• Per parameter: 2 bytes bf16 weights + 2 bytes gradients + 12 bytes fp32 master weights, momentum, variance = about 16 bytes.
• 7B x 16 bytes ≈ 112 GB before activations, so it needs sharding (e.g. ZeRO) across GPUs.
• Activations scale with batch x sequence x hidden x layers; reduce with activation checkpointing (recompute in backward).
• Inference needs only weights (about 14 GB in bf16) plus the KV cache.
cards.key_concept: Probe — LoRA fine-tuning needs no gradient or optimizer state for the frozen base weights, which is why it fits on far less hardware. It still stores activations for the backward pass, so activation memory does not shrink.

cards.title: Gradient accumulation and large batches
cards.question: What is gradient accumulation, and how should the learning rate change with batch size?
cards.answer:
• Accumulate gradients over several micro-batches before one optimizer step (as GPipe does), to simulate a larger batch without holding it in memory at once.
• Linear scaling rule: multiply LR by the batch-size factor, with warmup; breaks down beyond a point (about 8k images for ImageNet ResNet-50); the critical batch size sets the speed/efficiency trade-off.
cards.key_concept: Probe — BatchNorm statistics still use the micro-batch, and that batch size is part of the loss being optimized; LayerNorm has no batch-size dependence (it works at batch size 1), which suits small per-device batches.

cards.title: Recsys training at scale
cards.question: How do you train a model whose embedding tables do not fit on one device?
cards.answer:
• Hybrid parallelism: shard embedding tables across devices (model parallel: table-wise, row-wise for tables too big for one GPU, or column-wise), replicate the dense MLPs (data parallel); a personalized all-to-all exchanges embedding lookups.
• Cache frequently used embedding rows in fast GPU memory (LRU/LFU software cache in front of host memory); ID access is skewed toward popular items (power law).
cards.key_concept: Probe — Sharding strategy is a load-balancing problem: table-wise sharding is limited by skew in table sizes; row-wise balances better but its communication grows with the number of trainers; placement minimizes a cost of communication plus load imbalance.

cards.title: Backpropagation by hand
cards.question: A two-layer MLP: h = ReLU(W1 x + b1), logits z = W2 h + b2, loss = softmax cross-entropy against a one-hot y. Derive every gradient.
cards.answer:
• dL/dz = p - y, where p = softmax(z).
• dL/dW2 = (p - y) h^T. dL/db2 = p - y.
• dL/dh = W2^T (p - y). Through the ReLU: dL/da = dL/dh masked to the positions where a = W1 x + b1 is positive.
• dL/dW1 = (dL/da) x^T. dL/db1 = dL/da.
• For a batch, average over examples; with rows as examples the weight gradients become H^T (P - Y) / N and X^T (dL/dA) / N for weights stored as (in, out).
• Shape check: every gradient has the shape of the thing it is the gradient of.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How do you test a hand-written backward pass? Numerical gradient check: compare against (L(w + eps) - L(w - eps)) / (2 eps) for a few random entries, in float64. Practical ML coding rounds reward doing this unprompted.

cards.title: Implementing attention
cards.question: You are asked to implement causal multi-head self-attention from scratch. What are the shapes, and where do bugs hide?
cards.answer:
• Input (B, T, C). Project to Q, K, V, then reshape each to (B, heads, T, C / heads).
• Scores = Q K^T / sqrt(head_dim), shape (B, heads, T, T). Apply the causal mask before the softmax by setting positions j > i to negative infinity.
• Softmax over the last axis, multiply by V, move heads back and reshape to (B, T, C), then the output projection.
• Usual bugs: masking after the softmax, softmax over the wrong axis, a mask that is transposed (so tokens see the future and training loss looks too good), reshaping without first swapping the head and time axes, and forgetting to mask padding.
• Test: changing a later token must not change the outputs at earlier positions.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Your training loss falls to near zero in a few hundred steps on a language-modelling task. What do you suspect first? Leakage of the future through the mask, or targets that are not shifted by one position.

cards.title: Agents and tool use
cards.question: How does an LLM agent with tools work, how does it fail, and how do you evaluate it?
cards.answer:
• Loop: the model reads the conversation plus tool descriptions, emits either an answer or a structured tool call; the harness runs the tool and appends the result; repeat until the model answers or a step limit is hit.
• Failure modes: wrong tool or malformed arguments, loops and redundant calls, errors compounding over long tasks (per-step reliability multiplies), context filling with tool output, and prompt injection through tool results or retrieved documents.
• Mitigations: clear tool descriptions and schemas, returning errors the model can act on, trimming or summarising tool output, step and cost limits, human checkpoints before risky or irreversible actions, and treating tool output as data, not instructions.
• Evaluation: end-to-end task success on realistic tasks with checkable end states, run several times because outcomes vary; also cost, steps and latency per task, and a review of failed transcripts.
cards.key_concept: Probe — A task needs 20 steps and each step succeeds 95% of the time. How often does the task succeed with no recovery? 0.95^20 is about 36%. That is why agents need to detect and recover from their own errors, and why evaluating single steps overstates end-to-end quality.

cards.title: Two-proportion test by hand
cards.question: Control: 10,000 users, 1,000 convert. Treatment: 10,000 users, 1,080 convert. Is the lift significant at 5%, and what is the 95% interval?
cards.answer:
• Rates: 10.0% and 10.8%. Difference = 0.8 percentage points (an 8% relative lift).
• Standard error of the difference = sqrt(p1 (1 - p1) / n1 + p2 (1 - p2) / n2) = sqrt(0.1 x 0.9 / 10000 + 0.108 x 0.892 / 10000) ≈ sqrt(0.000009 + 0.00000963) ≈ 0.00432.
• z = 0.008 / 0.00432 ≈ 1.85, below 1.96, so not significant at 5% two-sided (p ≈ 0.064).
• 95% interval: 0.008 ± 1.96 x 0.00432 ≈ (-0.05, +1.65) percentage points. It includes zero.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What do you tell the product manager? The data are consistent with anything from no effect to a 1.6-point lift. If a lift of this size would matter, the test was underpowered: about 16 x 0.1 x 0.9 / 0.008^2 ≈ 22,500 users per arm are needed for 80% power, so run it longer.

cards.title: Causal inference without an experiment
cards.question: You cannot run an A/B test. Name the main ways to estimate a causal effect from observational data and what each assumes.
cards.answer:
• Difference-in-differences: compare the change over time in a treated group with the change in an untreated group. Assumes the two would have moved in parallel without the treatment.
• Propensity methods (matching, inverse propensity weighting): model the probability of treatment given covariates and balance the groups on it. Assumes no unmeasured confounders and that every kind of unit had some chance of either treatment.
• Instrumental variables: use something that changes treatment but affects the outcome only through it (for example a randomised nudge). Assumes that exclusion holds; estimates the effect for those the instrument moves.
• Regression discontinuity: compare units just either side of a threshold that assigns treatment. Assumes nothing else changes at the threshold; estimates a local effect.
• Synthetic control: build a weighted mix of untreated units that tracked the treated unit before the change.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Which assumption can you test? Parallel trends itself cannot be tested, but pre-treatment trends (event study) and covariate balance can be checked; no unmeasured confounding cannot be. Say so, and run a placebo or falsification test.

cards.title: Off-policy estimators
cards.question: Compare the direct method, inverse propensity scoring, self-normalised IPS and doubly robust estimation for evaluating a new recommendation policy on logged data.
cards.answer:
• Direct method: fit a reward model and average its predictions under the new policy. Low variance, but often much larger bias wherever the reward model is wrong.
• IPS: average of reward x (new policy probability / logging probability) over logged actions. Unbiased if propensities are correct and the logging policy has full support (every action the new one can take gets some probability); variance explodes as logging probabilities get small.
• Self-normalised IPS: divide by the sum of the weights instead of n. Biased but consistent, bounded within the reward range, and more accurate when weight fluctuations dominate. Clipping weights trades bias for variance in the same spirit.
• Doubly robust: direct-method estimate plus an IPS-weighted correction of its residuals. Unbiased if either the reward model or the propensities are right, and usually lower variance than IPS.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why do these struggle for ranked lists? The action is a whole slate, so the exact logged slate has a tiny propensity. Practical answers are estimators with position-level assumptions (e.g. examination depends only on rank), small action spaces, or interleaving and A/B tests for the final call.

cards.title: Model choice
cards.question: Tell me about a model you shipped. Why that model and not a simpler one?
cards.answer:
• Name the baseline (a heuristic or a linear model) and its number on the metric that mattered.
• Give the lift of the shipped model over it, offline and online.
• Say what the complexity cost: latency, serving cost, on-call burden, iteration speed.
• Name one alternative you rejected and the evidence that decided it.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Would you make the same choice today? A staff-level answer changes something and says what you learned.

cards.title: Labels
cards.question: What was the label for that model, where did it come from, and how could it be wrong?
cards.answer:
• Define the label exactly, including the time window.
• Say who or what produced it (user action, human rater, downstream system) and how delayed it was.
• Name its biases: selection by the previous model, position, missing negatives, rater disagreement.
• Say what you did about one of them and how you measured the effect.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How did you know the label tracked what the business cared about? Name the validation: a correlation study, a holdout, a survey.

cards.title: Offline versus online
cards.question: Describe a time offline metrics and the A/B test disagreed.
cards.answer:
• State both results with numbers.
• Give your hypotheses in the order you tested them (skew, selection bias, metric mismatch, novelty).
• Say what the evidence showed and what you changed in the evaluation afterwards.
• Say what you shipped, or did not, and why.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What do you now check before trusting an offline win?

cards.title: Failure in production
cards.question: Tell me about a model or pipeline of yours that failed in production.
cards.answer:
• What users or the business saw, and for how long.
• How it was detected: an alert you had built, or a person noticing.
• Root cause, in one sentence a non-specialist could follow.
• The immediate fix, then what you changed so that class of failure cannot recur.
• Your own part in the cause, stated plainly.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What would have caught it a day earlier?

cards.title: Scope and influence
cards.question: Describe a technical decision you drove across teams where people disagreed.
cards.answer:
• The decision and why it mattered beyond your team.
• The strongest version of the other side's position.
• What you did to resolve it: data, a prototype, a written proposal, a timeboxed experiment.
• The outcome, including what you conceded.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Which part of the result was yours and which was the team's? Be exact; interviewers probe for inflated ownership.

cards.title: Trade-offs under constraint
cards.question: What would you have done differently with half the time? With twice the time?
cards.answer:
• Half: what you would cut first and the risk that accepts.
• Twice: the one investment with the highest expected return, and why not the others.
• Show that the original plan was a choice among options, not the only path.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What did you deliberately not build, and has that decision held up?

cards.title: Why this company (Anthropic)
cards.question: Why do you want to work on AI at a company focused on safety, and what worries you about it?
cards.answer:
• A specific reason tied to your own work or reading, not a summary of the website.
• A view on at least one real risk or trade-off, held with reasons and stated with its uncertainty.
• Evidence you have read primary material: the company's published research or policies. Read them before the interview.
• How the role you are applying for connects to that.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Where do you disagree with the company's approach? Having no disagreement reads as not having thought about it.

cards.title: Feedback and candour (Netflix)
cards.question: Tell me about hard feedback you gave a peer or a manager, and hard feedback you received.
cards.answer:
• The situation and why the feedback was needed.
• What you said, close to the actual words, and how you delivered it.
• What happened afterwards.
• For feedback received: what you changed, with a concrete before and after.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Netflix's culture memo lists Candor as one of its values: “You willingly receive and give feedback; you are open about what’s working and what needs to improve; you admit mistakes openly and share learnings widely.” It asks for “extraordinary candor”, with constructive feedback part of everyday work, says this is especially hard when the feedback goes to someone more senior or from a different background, and asks people to say things about a colleague only if they are willing to say them to that colleague directly. Prepare one story of feedback given upward and one of feedback received that changed what you do. The memo's other values: Selflessness, Judgment, Creativity, Courage, Inclusion, Curiosity, Resilience.

cards.title: Judgment without process
cards.question: Describe a decision you made without asking permission that carried real risk.
cards.answer:
• The context you had and how you got it.
• Why you judged it yours to make, and who you informed.
• The outcome, good or bad.
• What you would do the same and differently.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How do you decide when to act and when to ask? Give your actual rule. At Netflix, the culture memo's “People Over Process” section names an “informed captain” for every significant decision, who seeks out dissenting opinions (“farming for dissent”) and then makes the call; everyone else is expected to “disagree then commit”, and managers practise “context not control”.

cards.title: Depth check
cards.question: Pick the most technically difficult part of your last project and teach it to me.
cards.answer:
• Start from the problem, not the solution.
• One level of detail deeper than feels necessary: the equation, the data structure, the failure case.
• What you tried that did not work.
• What you still do not understand about it.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Interviewers keep asking "why" until you reach the edge of what you know. Saying "I don't know, here is how I would find out" at that edge is the right answer.
